familyProfiles/catholic/tagline: The world's largest church, united with the Bishop of Rome.
familyProfiles/catholic/summary: The communion of Latin and Eastern Catholic churches in full communion with the Pope as successor of Peter. It holds Scripture and Tradition as interpreted by the magisterium, seven sacraments, and a worldwide structure of dioceses that make it the largest single Christian body.
familyProfiles/catholic/story:
The Catholic Church traces its origins to the apostles, and especially to Peter and Paul at Rome; the bishops of Rome claimed a leading role from early on, and Leo I (440–461) and Gregory I (590–604) gave the papacy its classic shape. After the fall of the Western Empire, monks and missionaries carried Latin Christianity to the Germanic, Celtic, Slavic and Scandinavian peoples. The mutual excommunications of 1054 are the conventional date of separation from the Orthodox East, though the estrangement was gradual.

The medieval Western church created universities, religious orders (Benedictines, Cistercians, Franciscans, Dominicans), canon law and scholastic theology. Its authority was shaken by the Avignon papacy and the Great Western Schism (1378–1417) and then broken in much of northern Europe by the Protestant Reformation. The Council of Trent (1545–63) answered with a reformed, confessional Catholicism, while Jesuits and other orders carried the faith to the Americas, Africa and Asia, including Goa (1510) and the Fisher Coast of Tamil Nadu under Francis Xavier (1542).

Modern Catholicism was shaped by the First Vatican Council (1869–70), which defined papal infallibility and led to the Old Catholic separation, and by the Second Vatican Council (1962–65), which introduced vernacular liturgy, ecumenism and a new engagement with the modern world. Traditionalist resistance to the council produced the Society of St Pius X (1970). Twenty-three Eastern Catholic churches, such as the Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Maronite and Syro-Malabar churches, share the communion while keeping their own rites and laws.

The Vatican's statistical office counted 1,422,144,000 Catholics at the end of 2024, about 17.8 per cent of the world's population. Nearly half (47.7 per cent) live in the Americas, and Africa (20.3 per cent) now slightly outnumbers Europe (20.2 per cent); Brazil, Mexico, the Philippines, the United States and the Democratic Republic of Congo have among the largest Catholic populations.

Catholic influence extends through the largest non-governmental network of schools, hospitals and charities in the world, a body of social teaching beginning with Rerum Novarum (1891), and an intellectual tradition from Augustine and Aquinas to the present. Anglican, Lutheran and other Protestant traditions were formed in reaction to it and still share much of its liturgy and doctrine.
familyProfiles/catholic/origin/event: Mutual excommunications between Rome and Constantinople mark the conventional break with the East; the church of Rome itself traces its line to Peter and Paul.
familyProfiles/catholic/coreDoctrines/0: Revelation is handed on in Scripture and Tradition, authentically interpreted by the magisterium of the bishops with the Pope.
familyProfiles/catholic/coreDoctrines/1: The Pope, as successor of Peter, has universal jurisdiction and, under defined conditions, infallibility (Vatican I, 1870).
familyProfiles/catholic/coreDoctrines/2: Seven sacraments, with the Eucharist as the 'source and summit' of Christian life and Christ substantially present (transubstantiation).
familyProfiles/catholic/coreDoctrines/3: Justification by grace, received in faith and baptism and expressed in charity (Council of Trent, 1547).
familyProfiles/catholic/coreDoctrines/4: Veneration of Mary and the saints, including the Immaculate Conception (1854) and Assumption (1950) of Mary.
familyProfiles/catholic/coreDoctrines/5: Purgatory and the communion of saints, including prayer for the dead.
familyProfiles/catholic/focuses/0: The Mass and sacramental life of parishes.
familyProfiles/catholic/focuses/1: Unity of a worldwide church under bishops in communion with Rome.
familyProfiles/catholic/focuses/2: Catholic social teaching on human dignity, the common good and the poor.
familyProfiles/catholic/focuses/3: Education, health care and charity through orders and institutions.
familyProfiles/catholic/focuses/4: Defence of life from conception to natural death, and of marriage.
familyProfiles/catholic/strengths/0: Visible global unity across cultures and languages.
familyProfiles/catholic/strengths/1: Continuity of liturgy and doctrine across two millennia.
familyProfiles/catholic/strengths/2: Huge educational, medical and charitable network.
familyProfiles/catholic/strengths/3: Rich intellectual and spiritual traditions (Thomism, Carmelite mysticism, Ignatian spirituality).
familyProfiles/catholic/criticisms/0: Protestants and Orthodox reject the claims of papal primacy and infallibility.
familyProfiles/catholic/criticisms/1: Abuse scandals and their cover-up have badly damaged trust since the 1990s.
familyProfiles/catholic/criticisms/2: Historic involvement in the Inquisition, colonial conquest and coercion of dissenters.
familyProfiles/catholic/criticisms/3: Critics inside and outside question the exclusion of women from ordained ministry.
familyProfiles/catholic/internalDivision: Two and then three rival popes until the Council of Constance (1414–18).
Much of northern Europe left communion with Rome.
Augustinian rigorists condemned by Rome; the Church of Utrecht later went its own way.
Opponents of papal infallibility formed the Union of Utrecht (1889).
Filipino clergy broke with Spanish friars and Rome under Gregorio Aglipay.
Archbishop Lefebvre's unauthorised consecrations led to excommunications (lifted 2009) and an irregular status.
familyProfiles/catholic/influencedFamili: Lutheranism kept much of the Mass and sacramental theology while rejecting papal authority.
The Church of England retained Catholic orders, creeds and liturgical forms.
The Catholic Charismatic Renewal (from 1967) became one of the largest charismatic streams.
Many African and Philippine independent churches grew out of Catholic missions.
familyProfiles/orthodox/tagline: A family of self-governing churches keeping the faith of the seven councils.
familyProfiles/orthodox/summary: The communion of autocephalous churches, led by the Ecumenical Patriarch as 'first among equals', that accepts the seven ecumenical councils and the Byzantine liturgical tradition. It sees itself as the one, holy, catholic and apostolic church preserved without innovation.
familyProfiles/orthodox/story:
Eastern Orthodoxy is the continuation of the Greek-speaking church of the Byzantine Empire, centred on Constantinople and the ancient patriarchates of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. Its faith was shaped by the seven ecumenical councils from Nicaea (325) to Nicaea II (787), which restored the veneration of icons. Tensions with Rome over papal authority, the Filioque clause in the Creed and differing customs culminated in the excommunications of 1054 and, decisively, the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204.

Missionary work by Cyril and Methodius (863) gave the Slavs a liturgy in their own language; Bulgaria, Serbia and Kievan Rus' (baptised under Vladimir in 988) became Orthodox. After the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453, Moscow increasingly saw itself as the protector of Orthodoxy and gained a patriarchate in 1589. Russian missionaries later reached Siberia, Alaska, Japan and China.

Orthodoxy is organised by self-governing (autocephalous) national churches rather than a single central authority, and many of its divisions have been about who may grant independence and over which territory. Nineteenth-century nationalism produced new churches in Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria; the Bulgarian Exarchate was condemned for 'ethnophyletism' in 1872. The twentieth century brought Communist persecution, emigration and calendar disputes, and in 2018 the Moscow Patriarchate broke communion with Constantinople over the recognition of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine.

The Pew Research Center (2017) estimated about 260 million Orthodox Christians worldwide (a figure that includes the Oriental Orthodox churches); roughly 100 million live in Russia, with large populations in Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Serbia, Bulgaria, Belarus and Georgia, and growing diasporas in Western Europe, North America and Australia.

Orthodoxy has given the wider church the theology of the Cappadocian Fathers, Maximus the Confessor and Gregory Palamas, the art of the icon, the Jesus Prayer and the hesychast tradition gathered in the Philokalia, and a strong emphasis on theosis, or participation in the divine life, which has attracted renewed interest from Western Christians since the twentieth century.
familyProfiles/orthodox/origin/event: Mutual excommunications between Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Keroularios, the conventional date of the East–West schism.
familyProfiles/orthodox/coreDoctrines/0: Holy Tradition, of which Scripture is the heart, together with the seven ecumenical councils.
familyProfiles/orthodox/coreDoctrines/1: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father (rejecting the Western Filioque).
familyProfiles/orthodox/coreDoctrines/2: Salvation as theosis: union with God by grace through the sacraments and ascetic life.
familyProfiles/orthodox/coreDoctrines/3: The veneration of icons as affirmed by the Second Council of Nicaea (787).
familyProfiles/orthodox/coreDoctrines/4: The Eucharist as the true Body and Blood of Christ, celebrated in the Divine Liturgy.
familyProfiles/orthodox/coreDoctrines/5: Bishops are equal in sacramental rank; primacy is one of honour and coordination, not universal jurisdiction.
familyProfiles/orthodox/focuses/0: The Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom and the liturgical year.
familyProfiles/orthodox/focuses/1: Monasticism, with Mount Athos as a spiritual centre.
familyProfiles/orthodox/focuses/2: Prayer of the heart and the hesychast tradition.
familyProfiles/orthodox/focuses/3: Preservation of the faith unchanged from the Fathers.
familyProfiles/orthodox/focuses/4: The church as the bearer of national and cultural identity.
familyProfiles/orthodox/strengths/0: Deep liturgical and mystical tradition with continuity from late antiquity.
familyProfiles/orthodox/strengths/1: Survived Ottoman rule and Communist persecution.
familyProfiles/orthodox/strengths/2: Theology of theosis and the Holy Spirit valued across traditions.
familyProfiles/orthodox/strengths/3: Conciliar and local structure that keeps worship in vernacular cultures.
familyProfiles/orthodox/criticisms/0: Close ties between churches and nation-states, including support for governments in war.
familyProfiles/orthodox/criticisms/1: Jurisdictional rivalry, especially in the diaspora and in Ukraine.
familyProfiles/orthodox/criticisms/2: Slowness to adapt, and resistance to ecumenism in some quarters.
familyProfiles/orthodox/criticisms/3: Limited roles for women, with no ordained women priests.
familyProfiles/orthodox/internalDivision: Russian traditionalists rejected Patriarch Nikon's liturgical reforms.
Constantinople condemned 'phyletism' when Bulgarians organised their own church; healed 1945.
Adoption of the Revised Julian calendar in Greece produced Old Calendarist groups.
Émigré bishops separated from Moscow; communion restored in 2007.
Holy and Great Council of Crete
Moscow, Antioch, Bulgaria and Georgia stayed away from the long-planned pan-Orthodox council.
Moscow broke communion after Constantinople moved to grant autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (2019).
familyProfiles/orthodox/influencedFamili: Eastern Catholic churches keep Byzantine worship; Vatican II drew on Orthodox theology.
Anglican divines and the Oxford Movement looked to the Greek Fathers; long Anglican–Orthodox dialogue.
John Wesley drew on Eastern writers such as Macarius in his teaching on holiness.
familyProfiles/oriental/tagline: Ancient non-Chalcedonian churches of Egypt, Ethiopia, Armenia, Syria and India.
familyProfiles/oriental/summary: The Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac and Malankara (Indian) Orthodox churches, which accept the first three ecumenical councils but not Chalcedon (451). They confess the one incarnate nature of God the Word, following Cyril of Alexandria, and are in communion with each other but not with the Eastern Orthodox.
familyProfiles/oriental/story:
The Oriental Orthodox churches are the heirs of those who rejected the Council of Chalcedon in 451. Following Cyril of Alexandria and later Severus of Antioch, they insisted that Christ is one incarnate nature of God the Word, united without confusion or division, and suspected the council's 'in two natures' of dividing Christ. Opponents called them 'Monophysites'; they reject the label, preferring 'Miaphysite'. Language, regional loyalties and resentment of Byzantine imperial power deepened the separation.

These churches were already rooted in ancient nations. Armenia had adopted Christianity under Tiridates III and Gregory the Illuminator (traditionally 301), and Ethiopia under King Ezana around 330. In Egypt the Coptic Church kept its own patriarch of Alexandria, and in Syria Jacob Baradaeus (d. 578) organised a separate hierarchy, giving the Syriac Orthodox the nickname 'Jacobites'. In India, Thomas Christians who rejected Portuguese Latinisation at the Coonan Cross Oath (1653) later received bishops from the Syriac Orthodox patriarch.

Most of these churches lived for centuries under Muslim rule, as minorities with protected but subordinate status. They suffered heavy losses in the twentieth century, above all in the Armenian genocide (1915) and the Assyrian and Syriac massacres of the same years, and more recently in the wars in Iraq and Syria. Internal divisions have mostly been over jurisdiction: the Malankara church in India split between those loyal to the Antiochian patriarch and those claiming autocephaly, and Eritrea's church became independent of Ethiopia's after 1993.

The largest is the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, to which 43.5 per cent of Ethiopians (about 32 million) declared adherence in the 2007 census. The Coptic Church remains the largest Christian body in the Middle East, and the Armenian, Syriac and Indian churches have substantial diasporas.

The family preserved some of the oldest forms of Christian worship, the Desert Fathers' monasticism (born in Egypt), unique biblical canons and literatures in Ge'ez, Coptic, Armenian and Syriac, and the faith of the Kerala Christians. Joint statements with the Eastern Orthodox (1989–90) and the Catholic Church (e.g. 1973, 1984) concluded that the Christological disagreement was largely one of terminology.
familyProfiles/oriental/origin/event: Rejection of the Council of Chalcedon's definition of Christ 'in two natures' by much of Egypt, Syria and Armenia.
familyProfiles/oriental/coreDoctrines/0: Christ is one incarnate nature of God the Word, fully divine and fully human (Cyril of Alexandria).
familyProfiles/oriental/coreDoctrines/1: Acceptance of the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus only.
familyProfiles/oriental/coreDoctrines/2: Seven sacraments (mysteries), with the Eucharist as the true Body and Blood of Christ.
familyProfiles/oriental/coreDoctrines/3: Holy Tradition, the Fathers and the liturgy as the context for Scripture.
familyProfiles/oriental/coreDoctrines/4: Veneration of the Theotokos and the saints, with extensive fasting.
familyProfiles/oriental/focuses/0: Ancient liturgies in Coptic, Ge'ez, Armenian, Syriac and Malayalam.
familyProfiles/oriental/focuses/2: Long fasting seasons (Ethiopian Orthodox fast more than 180 days a year).
familyProfiles/oriental/focuses/3: Survival and identity as minority or national churches.
familyProfiles/oriental/strengths/0: Among the oldest continuous Christian communities in the world.
familyProfiles/oriental/strengths/1: Rich liturgical, musical and artistic traditions.
familyProfiles/oriental/strengths/2: Endurance through centuries of minority status and persecution.
familyProfiles/oriental/strengths/3: Fruitful Christological dialogues with Eastern Orthodox and Catholics.
familyProfiles/oriental/criticisms/0: Chalcedonian churches historically regarded their Christology as heretical.
familyProfiles/oriental/criticisms/1: Jurisdictional disputes, especially in Kerala, have led to long litigation.
familyProfiles/oriental/criticisms/2: Strong identification with ethnicity can limit outreach.
familyProfiles/oriental/criticisms/3: Little ordained ministry for women (though deaconesses are being revived in some places).
familyProfiles/oriental/internalDivision: Two Armenian catholicosates (Etchmiadzin and Cilicia) emerged; both remain in communion but are rivals in the diaspora.
Division in Kerala between supporters of an autocephalous catholicos and loyalists to the Syriac patriarch; Indian Supreme Court ruling in 2017.
The Ethiopian church received its own patriarch, ending its dependence on the Coptic Church.
The Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church became independent of Ethiopia after Eritrean independence.
A rival synod abroad after the deposition of Patriarch Merkorios; reconciled in 2018.
familyProfiles/oriental/influencedFamili: Christological dialogue since 1964 has reshaped Eastern Orthodox understanding of the 451 schism.
Coptic, Ethiopian, Syriac, Armenian and Syro-Malankara Catholic churches grew out of these traditions.
Ethiopia's ancient church inspired the 'Ethiopian' independent churches of southern Africa from 1892.
